headline: High: shared git/workspace and overlapping write/network capabilities make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes repo files and shares state via a git repo; TREK uses MCP and real-time collaboration, so content from one can plausibly flow into the other through shared files or copied outputs. No direct provenance controls are documented, but the bridge is not purely manual.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or synced workspace, injected instructions in files can reach the other agent.
IF TREK ingests MCP or collaborative messages without provenance tagging, attacker-controlled text can be treated as instructions.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable MCP paths that ingest untrusted text.
Require explicit human review before applying file-based instructions.
Add provenance labels to shared artifacts.
Use read-only handoff files for inter-agent communication.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider has broad network egress and handles model-provider API keys; TREK touches reservations, documents, photos, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets. If they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive travel data can be exposed to external model providers or logs by default. The pairwise leakage path is plausible even without extra configuration.
conditions: IF Aider is pointed at a repo containing TREK data files, those contents can be sent to configured model providers.
IF TREK stores secrets or reservations in shared files, Aider can read them from the filesystem.
mitigations: Keep TREK secrets out of the shared repo.
Use separate OS users or containers.
Redact sensitive files before Aider access.
Restrict Aider model-provider credentials to non-sensitive projects.
Rotate any exposed API keys or MFA secrets.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can write the filesystem and modify git state; TREK is collaborative and uses files plus WebSocket/MCP-backed state. If both touch the same repo or mutable workspace, concurrent writes and git changes can conflict and overwrite each other. The profiles document enough overlap to treat this as dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same git repository, concurrent edits can clobber each other.
IF TREK persists collaborative state in shared files while Aider auto-commits, merge conflicts can corrupt work.
mitigations: Assign separate branches per agent.
Enable file-level locking or a single-writer policy.
Pause one agent during the other's commit window.
Use automated conflict detection before merge.
Mirror shared state into append-only logs.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider can generate code changes that TREK may consume as collaborative input or documentation, and TREK has real-time collaborative workflows that can propagate those outputs. However, the profiles do not show TREK automatically executing Aider's output, so the main risk is unverified propagation rather than direct harmful action.
conditions: IF TREK treats Aider-authored text or files as authoritative, errors can cascade into shared plans or records.
IF Aider-generated edits are copied into TREK without review, downstream users may act on incorrect content.
mitigations: Require review of Aider outputs before import.
Mark machine-generated content clearly.
Add validation checks for structured fields.
Limit TREK actions to confirmed user inputs.
Keep a rollback path for imported changes.

E_compliance.rationale: Aider is docs-only and handles source code plus git history, while TREK touches travel records, email addresses, reservations, and MFA secrets. That creates a plausible compliance mismatch around retention and sensitive personal data, especially if TREK data is stored in the same repo or logs. The profiles do not prove a specific residency breach, so medium is the higher justified level.
conditions: IF TREK personal data is stored in files Aider can read, retention and access controls may diverge.
IF logs or git history retain travel identifiers, deletion requests may not fully remove them.
mitigations: Exclude personal data from git history.
Set short log retention for TREK.
Store secrets outside shared repos.
Document a deletion/export workflow.
Review residency and DPA requirements before sharing data.
